claims.text: The baseline bulk HfNbTaTiZr is treated as a homogeneous, defect-free random solid solution.
Monte Carlo routines coupled with DFT/MD or CALPHAD can produce chemical short-range order in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed ordering preferentially enhances Hf-Ti and Ti-Zr clustering.
Preferential Hf-Ti and Ti-Zr clustering produces percolative pathways.
The high-temperature comparison concerns an HfNbTaTiZr specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Electrical transport in the 0–200 K regime is less affected by oxygen impurities than transport at higher temperatures.
Chemical short-range order creates local inhomogeneities that establish enhanced electron-conduction paths.
Percolation networks better represent the local atomic environments and impurity effects governing electrical conduction.
Explicit treatment of short-range order will make predicted conductivity more accurate than conventional defect-free analytical models over 0–200 K.
Explicit treatment of short-range order will make predicted conductivity more accurate than conventional defect-free analytical models over 300–1200 K.
The proposed approach will reduce predictive error by approximately 15–20% relative to conventional analytical predictions.
The high-temperature simulations will account for conductivity modifications caused by 1 wt.% oxygen.
Existing analytical approaches assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
Defect-free analytical approaches deviate notably from measured HfNbTaTiZr conductivity, particularly with oxygen impurities and at temperature extremes.
The model is applicable to bulk, near-equilibrium HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen levels around 1 wt.% within 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The model may not be reliable at higher impurity concentrations or for processing histories that substantially alter the defect landscape.
X-ray or neutron scattering can reveal the proposed Hf-Ti and Ti-Zr clustering.
Failure to obtain at least an approximately 15–20% error reduction, or failure to observe the expected clustering and percolation signatures, would falsify the hypothesis.
